notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0120g.stoa003.opp-l: The parenthetical source references (Symmachus, Leo, Hilary, Gelasius, Gregory, etc.) are the editor's identifications of the borrowed passages in this forgery; they are kept as printed. Numerous scanning errors were silently corrected (e.g. 'Caroem' for carnem, 'inumubrante' for inumbrante, 'curporis' for corporis, 'monderandus' for moderandus/metiendus, 'falendi' for fallendi). The two references both numbered 1.2 are translated as separate lines. The Hilary-derived passage on the times of Christ's speech is obscure in the Latin and the rendering is close to literal. 'fabae tantum et uvae': 'beans' is odd, since the Apostolic Canons permit new ears of grain and grapes at the altar; the text may be corrupt, but it is translated as it stands. The consuls Aurelian and Marcellus correspond to no consular year in Eutychian's pontificate, as is typical of the Pseudo-Isidorian dates.

Several scanning errors read silently (e.g. 'Ire' for 'iræ', 'Wilti' for 'mihi', 'enuriet' for 'enutriet', 'iacet' for 'manet', 'Vox' for 'Vos'). In line 2.6 'custodiat similitudinem' is rendered as accepting the penalty of retaliation (talio) in case of false accusation. In 2.7 the sentence ending 'aut regulariter prohibita neglexerint' is elliptical; the bracketed supplement is conjectural. The dating 'Caro Secundo et Carino' is read as Carus consul for the second time with Carinus (283).

nodes.text: THE LETTER AND DECREES, OF DOUBTFUL AUTHENTICITY, OF SAINT EUTYCHIAN, POPE AND MARTYR.
TO JOHN AND TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF THE BAETICAN
On the faith of the Incarnation of the Lord.
That Christ, with the distinct character of each nature preserved, was true God and true man.
To his dearest brothers John and all the bishops established throughout the province of Baetica, Bishop Eutychian [sends] greeting in the Lord.

The fairness of your request urges us to assent gladly to the wish of your fraternity (Symmachus, letter 5, to St Caesarius), and to reply briefly to your inquiries. And although I know that your love is devoted to every good work (St Leo, letter 4C), yet so that it may be more effective toward those who do not think soundly, we instruct [you] how you ought to inform them about the incarnation of our Saviour. This, then, is the one immovable foundation, this the one blessed rock of faith, confessed by the mouth of Peter: 'You are,' he says, 'the Christ, the Son of the living God' (St Matthew 16); it holds within itself as many proofs of truth as there will be questions of perversity and slanders of unbelief raised against it (St Leo, p. 97, from the books of St Hilary On the Trinity, which he cites). In everything else, now, let it be the dispensation of the Father's will. Therefore the birth and the body, and after that the cross, death, and hell, are our salvation. For for the sake of the human race the Son of God was born of the Virgin and of the Holy Spirit; and, with the Spirit himself serving him in this work, and with his own, that is God's, overshadowing power, he sowed for himself the beginnings of a body and established the first stages of flesh, so that, made man from a virgin, he might take the nature of flesh into himself, so that through the fellowship of this mingling the body of the whole human race might be sanctified in him. And just as all were founded in him through his willing to be bodily, so in turn he himself might be carried back into all through that in him which is invisible. The invisible image of God therefore did not refuse the shame of a human beginning, and passed through conception, birth, crying, and the cradle, and all the indignities of our nature. What, then, worthy of so great a condescension will we repay? The one only-begotten God, therefore, of an origin from God beyond telling, is implanted in the womb of the holy Virgin and grows into the form of a human body; he who contains all things, within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth by the law of human birth. He at whose voice archangels and angels tremble, and heaven and earth and all the elements of this world are dissolved, is heard in the crying of infancy. He who is invisible and incomprehensible, not to be measured by sight, sense or touch, is wrapped in a cradle. If anyone reflects that these things are unworthy of God, he confesses himself indebted for a kindness all the greater, the less these things befitted the majesty of God. He through whom man was made had no need to become man; but we had need that God should become flesh and dwell in us, that is, that by the assumption of flesh one should inhabit the inner parts of all flesh. His humility is our nobility; his indignity is our honour. What he is, God existing in flesh, that we in turn are, renewed from flesh into God. Clearly he does not know his own life who does not know that Christ Jesus is true man just as he is true God. And it is a matter of the same danger not to believe that Jesus Christ or the Holy Spirit is God, or to deny the flesh of our body in Christ (the same St Leo, in the same place, from the same St Hilary). 'Everyone therefore,' he says, 'who confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I will deny him before my Father who is in heaven' (Matthew 10). These things the Word made flesh (St John 1) spoke, and the man Jesus Christ, the Lord of majesty, taught, he who was himself established in himself as mediator for the salvation of the Church; and by that very mystery of the mediator between God and men, being one on both sides, since he, from natures united into the same, is one and the same reality of each nature; yet so that he lacked neither in either, lest by being born man he should cease to be God, or again, by remaining God, he should not be man. This, therefore, is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God and man, to confess Word and flesh; neither to be ignorant of God, that he is man, nor ignorant of the flesh, that it is the Word. The only-begotten God, therefore, born man of the virgin (the same, in the same letter, from the same St Hilary), and in the fullness of times about to advance man in himself into God, kept throughout this manner of gospel speech: that he taught himself to be believed the Son of God, and proclaimed and impressed upon [them] that he was the son of man, speaking and doing as man all the things that are God's, and then speaking and doing as God all the things that are man's; yet so that in that very speech of both kinds he never spoke except with the signification of both man and God. This, therefore, is an occasion for heretics to deceive the simple and ignorant, so that they falsely claim that what he said according to man was said according to a weakness of the divine nature; and because he who speaks all that he speaks about himself is one and the same, they contend that he spoke everything about the divinity. Nor indeed do we deny that all the speech that remains his is the speech of his own nature. But if Jesus Christ is both man and God, and neither was he first God only when he was man, nor, when he is both man and God, is he then not also God, nor after man in God is he not wholly man and wholly God, it must be said that the mystery of his [words] is one and the same as that of his kind. And when in him you distinguish man from God according to time, then distinguish the speech of God and of man. And when you confess God and man in time, then judge the sayings of God and of man in time. But when [it is the time] of man and God, again you understand the time of the whole man, now of the whole God; since that was said to show the time, the things said being fitted to the time: so that, since it is one thing that God is before man, another that he is man and God, another that after man and God he is wholly man and wholly God, you may not confuse the mystery of the dispensation by times and kinds, since, according to the quality of the kinds and natures, his speech in the mystery of man must have been one when not yet born, another when still about to die, another when eternal. Therefore Jesus Christ, doing all these things for our sake, and born a man of our body, spoke according to the custom of our nature, yet without omitting that it is of his own nature that he is God. For although in birth and passion and death he carried out the business of our nature, yet he did all those very things by the power of his own nature. Do you see that he so proclaimed God and man that death is assigned to the man, but the raising of the flesh to God? Yet not so that he who died is one, and he through whom the dead man rises is another. For despoiled of flesh, Christ died; and again, raising Christ from the dead, it is the same Christ, despoiling himself of flesh. Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; recognise the dispensation of man in death. And though both were done by their own natures, remember that he who is both is one Christ Jesus. These things therefore had to be shown by me in a few [words], so that we might remember that the form of each nature is treated in our Lord Jesus Christ: because he who, remaining in the form of God, took on the form of a servant, by no means lost his divinity. Furthermore, brothers, we urge you to warn them to turn to him. Whence it is written: 'Son, do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you. Do not be anxious about unjust riches: they will not profit you in the day of calamity and vengeance. Do not winnow yourself in every wind, and do not go in every way. For so the sinner is proved by a double tongue. Be steadfast in the way of the Lord, and in the truth of your understanding, and in knowledge: and let the word of peace and justice follow you. Be gentle in hearing the word of God, so that you may understand: and give answer with wisdom. If you have understanding, answer your neighbour: but if not, let your hand be upon your mouth, lest you be caught in an undisciplined word and be put to shame. Honour and glory are in the speech of the sensible man: but the tongue of the imprudent is his overthrow. Do not be called a whisperer, and do not be caught by your tongue and put to shame. For upon the thief come shame and repentance, and the worst condemnation upon the double-tongued: but upon the whisperer hatred, and enmity, and insult. Do justice to small and great alike. Do not become an enemy to your neighbour instead of a friend. For the wicked man will inherit reproach and insult, and so will every sinner who is envious and double-tongued. Do not exalt yourself in the thought of your soul like a bull, lest your strength be dashed down through folly: and it will eat your leaves, and destroy your fruit: and you will be left like a dry tree in the desert. For a wicked soul destroys the one who has it, and gives him over to the joy of his enemy, and leads him down into the lot of the ungodly' (Ecclesiasticus 6). With such exhortations, brothers, admonish one another, and always pursue good things and avoid evil ones. For with great care (Gelasius, letter 9), according to the blessed Apostle, we must take precautions lest the faith and teaching of the Lord be blasphemed (1 Timothy 6). And if those things must sometimes be allowed which, provided the soundness of the rest is assured, cannot by themselves do harm, yet those must be greatly guarded against which cannot be admitted without manifest disfigurement. But if those very things which are believed to be permissible at times without any harm are either forced by consideration of circumstances and times or excused by regard for urgent provision, how much more must those things in no way be curtailed which no necessity and no ecclesiastical advantage at all wrests from us? For this reason, brothers, we have set these things first, so that those kinds of produce which may not be offered on the altar, according to the constitution of the apostles and their successors (Apostolic Canons 3, 4, 5, from the version of Dionysius Exiguus), may be brought to the house of the priests, and blessed by the priests, and, having been blessed with a simple blessing, then be taken by the people: only beans and grapes, and the other things which the apostles appointed, are to be offered on the altar. We therefore desire (St Gregory, letter 52, book 4), dearest brothers, and beseech the almighty Lord with all our prayers, that he may make your love grow ever more fervent in the constancy of his love, and grant that you remain in one concord in the peace of the Church. We also admonish your fraternity (St Gregory, letter 25, book 2) to keep careful watch over the souls entrusted to you, and to attend more to the gains of souls than to the advantages of the present life. And in maintaining and managing the property of the Church be diligent guardians, so that the judge who is to come, when he comes to judge, may approve that you have in every respect worthily discharged the office of shepherd you have taken on. May almighty God keep you under his protection (St Gregory, letter 50, book 4), and grant that you preserve by your conduct the honour conferred on you by God, and help you to lead the souls entrusted to you, with manifold fruit, to the eternal pastures and to present them worthily to him, and deign to place you among his saints and elect. Given on the Ides of April, in the consulship of Aurelian and Marcellus, men of clarissimate rank.
TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SICILY.
I. On the manner of receiving an accusation against clerics.
II. Who are not to be admitted to the accusation of religious persons.
III. On the manner of proceeding in ecclesiastical business, since one ought not to proceed in the secular manner.
To his most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Sicily, Eutychian.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and unstained in his sight in love, predestining us to the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ unto himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he has shown us favour in his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the remission of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which has abounded in us in all wisdom and prudence, that he might make known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, those which are in the heavens and those which are on earth, in him. In whom we also have been called by lot, predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, that we may be to his praise and glory, we who before hoped in Christ: in whom you also, when you had heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation, in whom also believing you were sealed with the holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, unto the redemption of [his] possession, to the praise of his glory. Therefore I too, hearing of your faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, and your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making remembrance of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power in us who have believed, according to the working of the might of his power, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead, and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named not only in this age but also in the age to come. And he subjected all things under his feet, and gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body and his fullness: who fills all in all. And you, when you were dead in your offences and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit who now works in the sons of unbelief, among whom we too once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of the thoughts, and we were by nature sons of wrath, even as the rest. Now, brothers, because from sons of wrath God has by his grace and free mercy made us his sons: and we, who were not worthy [to be] servants, with no preceding merits, but by his grace (as we have said) have been made his sons: in whom we cry, Abba, Father: following his example, as sons of mercy and justice and love alike, that we may be able, with his help, to be called and to be true sons of God, laying aside (according to the apostle Peter) all malice and all deceit, and pretences, and envies, and all detractions. But those who do such things are proved to be not sons of God, but rather sons of the wicked one, as the Apostle Paul says: The works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, lust, the service of idols, poisonings, enmities, strifes, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and things like these, of which I forewarn you, as I have forewarned, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. Grave, brothers, and exceedingly dreadful is the word which he says: That those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. And the Truth himself says: What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, but suffer the loss of his own soul? Exceedingly grave are the things we have set out, and very greatly to be guarded against. For those to whom the kingdom of God is shut are without doubt also denied the Church. Of whom the Lord in the Gospel, announcing the power of the apostles and of their successors, says: Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you bind, they will be bound: that is, those whom you have barred from the Church, unless they have been reconciled through satisfaction, for them the door of the heavenly kingdom too will be shut.

I. Therefore, guarding against these things in advance, and foreseeing the minds of the foolish, with pastoral care, together with all the bishops and the faithful of both orders of the holy Roman and universal Church, we decree that ecclesiastical business is not to be conducted as secular business is. For under secular laws, once someone who has been summoned has come and has begun to contend in court, he may not withdraw before the case is concluded; but in ecclesiastical [business], when the case has been stated, he may withdraw if it is necessary, or if he sees himself being oppressed. And we declare and order to be kept the following order of accusation: that is, if any cleric is charged with a crime, he who could be accused is not at once to be considered guilty, lest we make innocence suspect. But whoever it is who brings the charge, let him come to judgement; let him name the accused; let him take on the bond of the written charge; let him accept the [penalty of] like for like; yet let him have the consideration due to his rank; nor let him suppose that he has licence to lie, since the likeness of punishment demands vengeance on calumniators. For all heretics, and suspects, and the excommunicated, murderers too and sorcerers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, and those who have committed abduction or given false testimony, or who have resorted to soothsayers and magicians, are by no means to be admitted to accusation.

II. Let no infamous or sacrilegious person ever be permitted, in any matter whatever, to give testimony against a religious Christian, however humble and servile a person he may be, nor to attack a Christian on any matter, by action or written charge. Likewise let the licence of accusing or testifying be denied to all who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, and the norm of their own law or their own profession, or [who have disregarded] what is forbidden by rule.

III. Likewise we forbid that any cases be heard by ecclesiastical judges which are not contained in the laws, or which are known to be prohibited. Not only ecclesiastical laws but also those of the world order these things to be observed. For accusation of priests ought not to be made indiscriminately and at random. For if it were readily admitted, very few indeed would be found: since all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution. But blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake. Hence the Truth himself says: Father, I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world. They were yours and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. Now they have known that all things which you gave me are from you: because the words which you gave me I have given to them, and they have received [them]: and they have known truly that I came forth from you, and they have believed that you sent me. I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you gave me, because they are yours. And all mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them. And now I am no longer in the world, and these are in the world, and I come to you. Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you gave me, that they may be one, as we also [are]. While I was with them, I kept them in your name. Those whom you gave me I guarded: and none of them perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled. But now I come to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word: and the world has hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. Sanctify them in the truth. Your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, I too have sent them into the world. And for them I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth. Yet I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, and the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory which you gave me I have given them, that they may be one, as we also are one. I in them, and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one, that the world may know that you sent me, and I have loved them as you also loved me. Father, those whom you gave me, I will that where I am, they too may be with me, that they may see my glory which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world. Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me. And I have made your name known to them, and will make it known, that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them. And the same John, apostle and evangelist, speaks in his first letter, saying: Dearest ones, let us love one another, for love is from God: and everyone who loves is born of God, and knows God. He who does not love does not know God, for God is love. In this the love of God appeared in us, that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, that we may live through him. In this is love, not as though we had loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins. Dearest ones, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us. In this we understand that we abide in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as saviour of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him and he in God. And we have seen and believed the love which God has in us. God is love: and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him. In this love is perfected with us, that we may have confidence on the day of judgement, because as he is, so are we in this world. There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. And he who fears is not perfect in love. Let us therefore love God, because God first loved us. If anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. For he who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And this commandment we have from God, that he who loves God should love his brother also. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. And everyone who loves him who begot loves also him who is born of him. In this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and do his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not burdensome. And through the prophet the Lord, warning that his disciples and their successors not be harmed, says: The angel of the Lord encircles round about those who fear him, and will rescue them. Taste and see that the Lord is good. Blessed is the man who hopes in him. Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for there is no want for those who fear him. Lions have been in need and gone hungry: but to those who seek the Lord no good thing will be lacking. Come, sons, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life, [who] loves to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit. Turn from evil, and do good: seek peace, and pursue it. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their cry. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth. The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their troubles. The Lord is near to the broken in heart, and will save the crushed in spirit. Many are the evils of the righteous, and from all of them the Lord will deliver him. The Lord keeps all his bones; not one of them will be broken. Malice will slay the wicked, and those who hate the righteous will be found guilty. The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants, and will set them free. You therefore, brothers, set your hearts upon the Lord, and he will nourish you, for he will not allow the righteous to waver for ever. But God our Lord will bring down our enemies, according to the Prophet's word, into the pit of destruction, for men of blood and deceit will not live out half their days. But you, always hope in the Lord, and have confidence in him, for he will deliver us. For he is blessed from age to age, and of his kingdom there will be no end. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October (in the year 283), in the consulship of Carus, for the second time, and Carinus, men of clarissimate rank.
